- Evaluation: Measure OOD accuracy and calibration (ECE); run a small human spot‑check for hallucinations; compare vs. naive full‑fine‑tune and zero‑shot baselines.

- WAREX is a plug‑and‑play reliability layer that injects realistic website/network failures (e.g., XSS pop‑ups, HTTPS and server‑side issues, layout changes) into existing web‑agent benchmarks (WebArena, WebVoyager, REAL) to measure robustness. The paper reports significant drops in task success rates under these conditions, highlighting brittleness in current agents.

Practical implications (3)
1) Reliability stress testing: Teams can add WAREX to existing evals to quantify how fragile their browser agents are to real‑world web instability without designing new tasks.
2) Hardening loop: Use WAREX in CI to catch regressions and guide mitigations (popup handling, DOM change tolerance, network retry/backoff, content‑security constraints) before deployment.
3) Comparable metrics across benchmarks: Because it integrates with WebArena/WebVoyager/REAL, organizations can baseline and track robustness alongside standard success‑rate metrics.

Caveat
- Early arXiv v1; coverage is limited to selected benchmarks and simulated failure modes (desktop web). Results may not generalize to mobile, anti‑bot defenses, or other dynamic sites without further extension.

text:
Hello team, I'm proposing a new workflow to improve our collaboration and avoid the persistent issues we've faced with real-time editing tools. Here is the text of a document I've prepared that outlines a Git-based workflow for our collaborative documentation. I believe this will provide a more stable and reliable platform for our work. Please review the following proposal.

Title: Git Workflow for Collaborative Documentation

For collaborations:
1. Make a repository on GitHub
2. Give your collaborators access to that GitHub repository.
3. Each of you write out issues for the project work.
4. Assign yourself an issue
5. Clone the repo to your local computer.
6. Create a branch, then work as normal, adding and committing files as you work.
7. Push your work to a pull request, which can be on `draft` mode if you are still working (so no one can merge it in prematurely).
8. Make sure you also `pull` the repository frequently to make sure you are always working with the most up-to-date version of the repository there is.

For individuals:
1. Make a repository on GitHub
   * you can also write issues or use the project boards for organization, though it's more for your benefit than anyone else's
2. Clone it to your local computer.
3. Work as normal, adding and committing files as you work
4. Push to GitHub minimum 1x/day but preferably like twice before and after lunch
   * If anyone wants to collaborate with you, they will need to fork your repository before making a pull request.
